The PointsIncentive contract treats reward as a raw token amount, but the target contract (venue) may expect a scaled representation (e.g., 18-decimal ERC20 vs. 6-decimal stablecoin) or a different semantic meaning (e.g., points vs. tokens). If the venue contract expects a normalized or scaled value (e.g., reward * 1e18) but receives raw units, the recipient receives a drastically incorrect amount. For example, if reward = 1000 and the venue contract expects 18 decimals, the recipient receives 1000 wei instead of 1000 tokens (1e21 wei), resulting in a 1e18x underpayment. This breaks the incentive promise and causes users to receive negligible or zero rewards, while the protocol appears to have fulfilled its obligation.
vulnerabilities.location: claim() function, line 46: (bool success,) = venue.call(abi.encodeWithSelector(selector, claimTarget, reward));

vulnerabilities.title: Claim Status Mapping Allows Reclaiming via Address Manipulation (Griefing)
vulnerabilities.description: The claimed mapping uses address as a key, but does not validate that claimTarget is a non-zero, non-contract, or non-malicious address. An attacker can repeatedly call claim() with different addresses that are not EOA (e.g., contract addresses, zero address, or randomly generated addresses) to fill the claimed mapping with invalid entries. Since the mapping is unbounded and each entry consumes ~200 gas and 32 bytes of storage, an attacker can exhaust the contract's storage capacity by making 10,000+ claims with non-user addresses. Once storage is saturated, legitimate users cannot claim because the contract cannot store new claimed flags, even if claims < limit. This is a denial-of-service attack that effectively locks out real users. For example, with 10,000 invalid claims, the contract uses 320 KB of storage — exceeding reasonable gas limits for future claims and making the incentive unusable.

vulnerabilities.title: Venue Ownership Check Is Incomplete and Allows Unauthorized Reward Issuance
vulnerabilities.description: The ownership check assumes that the venue contract uses a role-based system where role 1 (bit 1) grants issuance rights. However, the contract does not validate that the venue contract actually implements the expected role system or that role 1 corresponds to issuance. An attacker can deploy a malicious venue contract that returns true for hasAnyRole() for any address, or returns false for owner() but true for hasAnyRole() with an arbitrary role ID. This allows the attacker to impersonate an authorized caller and trigger reward issuance to themselves. For example, if reward = 10,000 tokens, the attacker calls claim() with their own address and a malicious venue contract, and receives 10,000 tokens without authorization. The economic impact is direct theft of the incentive pool funds.
vulnerabilities.location: claim() function, lines 38-39: if (points.owner() != address(this) && points.hasAnyRole(address(this), 1 << 1) != true) {

vulnerabilities.title: Arbitrary Fund Transfer via External Call Without Caller Verification
vulnerabilities.description: The claim() function executes an arbitrary external call to a user-specified contract (venue) with user-controlled selector and reward value, without verifying that the external call's destination or function is intended for legitimate reward issuance. This allows an attacker to trick the contract into sending funds to any arbitrary address via any function, effectively enabling unauthorized fund transfers. The contract assumes the venue contract is trusted and will only execute legitimate reward issuance, but no validation is performed on the selector or the target contract's behavior.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Authorization Bypass in Funds Destination Determination

vulnerabilities.title: Incomplete Operation Lifecycle: drawRaffle() Can Be Called Multiple Times Without Resetting State
vulnerabilities.description: The drawRaffle() function is declared but not implemented. This creates a critical lifecycle flaw: the raffle entries array is populated by users, but there is no mechanism to clear it after drawing a winner. This allows the same raffle to be drawn repeatedly, enabling an attacker to claim the reward multiple times if the reward is not properly consumed or if the contract allows re-entrancy or multiple draws.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing State Restoration in Raffle Lifecycle: Entries Array Never Cleared After Draw
vulnerabilities.description: When drawRaffle() is called (even if implemented), the entries[] array — which tracks all participants — is never cleared or reset. This means that after a winner is drawn, the same set of addresses remains in the array. If the incentive is reactivated or the contract is reused, subsequent calls to drawRaffle() will draw from the same pool, potentially re-awarding the same winner or allowing front-runners to predict outcomes. This violates the expectation that a raffle is a one-time event per incentive period.

vulnerabilities.title: Unimplemented Critical Function: drawRaffle() Leaves Raffle Logic Incomplete
vulnerabilities.description: The drawRaffle() function is declared as external and virtual but has no implementation. This means that for any instance using Strategy.RAFFLE, the incentive cannot be resolved. Users contribute to the raffle (via unspecified claim mechanism), but no winner can ever be selected. This renders the RAFFLE strategy completely non-functional, trapping the reward token in the contract indefinitely unless manually withdrawn by an admin — which is not part of the design.

vulnerabilities.title: Strategy Mismatch Risk: RAFFLE Strategy Has No Claim Mechanism Defined
vulnerabilities.description: The contract defines Strategy.RAFFLE but does not implement any function for users to enter the raffle (e.g., claim() or enterRaffle()). Without an entry mechanism, users cannot participate in the raffle, making the RAFFLE strategy unusable. This creates a logical inconsistency: the enum exists, the state variable is settable, but the lifecycle to populate entries[] is missing. This is a type system integrity failure in the contract’s design — the type system allows a state (RAFFLE) that cannot be meaningfully reached.
vulnerabilities.location: enum Strategy { POOL, RAFFLE } and absence of entry function

vulnerabilities.title: No Validation of Strategy State Before drawRaffle() Execution
vulnerabilities.description: The drawRaffle() function does not validate that strategy == Strategy.RAFFLE before attempting to draw. If an attacker or admin mistakenly sets strategy to POOL and calls drawRaffle(), the function will still execute (if implemented) and attempt to draw from entries[], which may be empty or improperly populated. This creates undefined behavior and potential reverts or incorrect winner selection. The function assumes the state is valid without checking, violating domain validation principles.
vulnerabilities.location: drawRaffle() function declaration (lacks modifier or require)

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Calculation Mismatch Between Claim and Clawback Leads to Fund Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The claim() function calculates the current reward using currentReward() and then updates state (lastClaimTime and currentReward) before transferring the reward. However, the clawback() function allows the owner to arbitrarily transfer any amount back to a target without validating it against the protocol's reward state. This enables the owner to clawback an amount greater than the current reward, effectively stealing funds from the incentive budget. The clawback function does not verify that the amount being returned matches the reward that was claimed, nor does it check against the currentReward() value or totalBudget. This creates a direct path for the owner to drain the contract's remaining balance by claiming a small reward, then clawing back the entire remaining balance as if it were a 'refund'.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Financial Loss via Unauthorized Fund Transfer

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call Creates Replayable Claim Vulnerability
vulnerabilities.description: The claim() function increments the claims counter and marks the recipient as claimed before executing the external call to the points contract. If the external call fails (e.g., due to insufficient balance, reentrancy, or malicious behavior in the venue contract), the state changes are already committed, preventing the same user from claiming again even though they received no reward. This allows an attacker to exhaust the claim limit by triggering failed claims, denying legitimate users their rewards.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing User Protection Against Partial Execution and Reward Loss
vulnerabilities.description: The claim() function performs an external call to an untrusted venue contract to distribute rewards, but provides no mechanism for the user to specify a minimum acceptable reward or to validate the outcome before committing state. If the venue contract reverts, executes incorrectly, or is malicious, the user loses their claim eligibility without receiving any reward. Users have no control over execution bounds, violating Pattern 1.

vulnerabilities.title: Validation Timing Violation: State Updated Before External Call Validation
vulnerabilities.description: The function updates state (claims++, claimed[claimTarget] = true) before validating the success of the external call to venue. This violates Pattern 2: validation (success of reward transfer) occurs after state change. If the external call fails, the user is permanently barred from claiming again, even though they received no reward. The validation of reward delivery happens too late.

vulnerabilities.title: External Contract Interface Assumption Without Verification
vulnerabilities.description: The contract assumes the venue contract implements a function with selector selector(address,uint256) that successfully transfers reward to claimTarget. However, no verification is performed that the venue contract actually executes the intended logic (e.g., it could be a dummy contract that accepts the call but does nothing). This violates Pattern 8: external system assumptions are not verified. An attacker could deploy a malicious venue contract that accepts the call but does not mint tokens, causing users to lose claims without reward.

vulnerabilities.title: Insecure Owner Authorization Check for Venue Contract
vulnerabilities.description: The authorization check for the venue contract only verifies if address(this) is the owner or has role 1<<1. However, role 1<<1 is not defined or documented, and the contract assumes a specific role structure in the venue contract without verifying its actual implementation. This creates a risk that the venue contract uses a different role system (e.g., from a forked protocol), making the authorization check ineffective. An attacker could exploit this to claim rewards from unauthorized venues.

vulnerabilities.title: Access Control Bypass on Reward Decay and Boost State Updates
vulnerabilities.description: The claim() function updates critical economic state variables (cgdaParams.lastClaimTime and cgdaParams.currentReward) without validating that the claimed reward amount is actually available in the contract's balance. An attacker can call claim() multiple times in rapid succession, causing the reward to decay below the actual available balance, leading to underpayment of legitimate claimants and potential insolvency. The state variables are updated unconditionally before the transfer, enabling a timing attack where the attacker manipulates the decay logic to reduce future rewards while still extracting the full current reward.

vulnerabilities.title: Unit Mismatch in Reward Calculation: Time-Based Boost Uses Seconds, Not Hours
vulnerabilities.description: The currentReward() function calculates reward boost using (timeSinceLastClaim * rewardBoost) / 3600, implying hourly increments. However, block.timestamp is in seconds, and the division by 3600 is mathematically correct for converting seconds to hours. The issue is not in the unit conversion itself, but in the representation boundary violation between the documented intent and the actual behavior: the contract's documentation states 'each hour adding rewardBoost', but the state variable cgdaParams.rewardBoost is defined as a per-hour boost amount. The problem arises because the rewardBoost value is set during initialization as a per-hour amount, but the calculation is applied continuously per second. This is not a unit error per se, but a representation boundary issue: the function returns a value that is mathematically correct for the given parameters, but the parameter interpretation is inconsistent with the documentation. However, a deeper issue exists: the rewardBoost is applied linearly over time, but the decay is applied discretely per claim. This creates a non-linear, unpredictable reward curve that can be exploited by attackers to front-run claims and manipulate the reward distribution. The real representation boundary violation is in the assumption that rewardBoost is a per-hour additive constant, but the calculation is continuous and the decay is discrete, leading to inconsistent economic behavior across time intervals.

vulnerabilities.title: Data Collection Integrity Violation: Claimed Status Not Reset on Clawback
vulnerabilities.description: The _isClaimable() function checks the claimed[recipient_] mapping to prevent double claims. However, the clawback() function transfers tokens back to a recipient without resetting the claimed[recipient_] flag. This means that if a clawback is performed (e.g., to correct an erroneous claim), the recipient is permanently marked as claimed and can never claim again, even if additional budget becomes available. This creates a data structure integrity violation where the claimed[] mapping becomes desynchronized with the actual claim eligibility. The claimed[] mapping is intended to prevent double claims, but it is not designed to be a permanent ban. This leads to permanent locking of user eligibility and loss of incentive utility.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Data Access and Collection Integrity Violation

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call Success Verification
vulnerabilities.description: The contract increments the claim counter and marks the recipient as claimed before verifying the success of the external call to the points contract. If the external call reverts (e.g., due to insufficient balance, reentrancy, or forked behavior), the claim state is permanently committed, but the reward is not delivered. This results in a permanent loss of claimability for the recipient and potential loss of reward tokens if the external contract fails to distribute them.

vulnerabilities.title: External Interface Compatibility Mismatch: Selector Usage Without Parameter Validation
vulnerabilities.description: The contract uses a dynamic selector (bytes4) to call an external points contract with two parameters: (address, uint256). However, the actual external points contract may expect additional parameters (e.g., a uint256 for claim ID, or a bytes32 for metadata) or may have a different signature (e.g., claim(address) or claim(address,uint256,uint256)). This ABI mismatch causes the external call to revert silently, but the state (claims++, claimed[recipient] = true) is already committed, permanently blocking the recipient from claiming again without reward delivery.

vulnerabilities.title: Authorization Context Not Bound to Execution Parameters
vulnerabilities.description: The contract authorizes any caller with owner or role 1<<1 to execute claim(), but the selector and reward are fixed at initialization. An attacker who gains access to the authorization (e.g., via compromised owner) can front-run legitimate claims by calling claim() with a different claimTarget while the original claim is pending. Since the authorization does not bind the claimTarget or reward value, the same authorization can be reused with arbitrary targets, enabling unauthorized reward distribution to malicious addresses.

vulnerabilities.title: Fork Behavioral Divergence: Assumed Points Contract Behavior May Not Hold on Forks
vulnerabilities.description: The contract assumes that calling venue with selector (address, uint256) will issue points to the recipient. However, on forks (e.g., from a base protocol like Balancer or Curve), the points issuance logic may have been moved to a separate distributor contract, or the function may now require a third parameter (e.g., epoch ID). Calling the original function on a forked contract may succeed (return true) but do nothing — no points are issued, no events emitted, and the reward is effectively burned. The claim state is still incremented, locking out the user.
